```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(jsurvival)
```

This guide describes the research methods in jsurvival 1.1.3. The small numerical
examples execute when this article is rendered. They check specific arithmetic and
output contracts; they do not validate every option or a clinical application.

## Choose the quantity before choosing the analysis

| Question | Quantity and analysis | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| How long until death from any cause? | Overall-survival Kaplan-Meier; Single Arm or Survival Analysis | Survival probability at a stated time |
| How often does one terminal cause occur with other terminal causes present? | Cumulative incidence in competing-risk mode | Probability of the specified cause by a stated time |
| Which baseline covariates are associated with hazard? | Multivariable Cox | Conditional hazard ratios, under proportional hazards |
| Which covariates are associated with cumulative incidence? | Multivariable Fine-Gray | Subdistribution hazard ratios, not probability ratios |
| How many events per observation time? | Person-time table | Crude events per person-time; no covariate adjustment |
| Which candidate predictors survive an L1 penalty? | LASSO Cox | Exploratory penalized coefficients and apparent performance |
| Which factors are associated with a binary endpoint? | Odds Ratio | Odds ratios; requires a defined outcome window and sampling design |

Kaplan-Meier and cumulative incidence are different estimands in the presence of competing
events. One minus cause-specific Kaplan-Meier is not the real-world probability of the
cause. See the survival authors' [competing-risk guide](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/survival/doc/compete.pdf).

DateTime Converter's native parsing-count percentages use all observations. For four
rows containing two valid dates, one missing value and one unparseable string, the
parsed share is 50%, missing is 25%, and failed is 25%. The separate parse rate among
non-missing values is 2/3 (66.7%). A high parse rate cannot verify the date order.

## Check the risk sets and rate denominator

Six independent patients have the following times. At time 2, an event and a censoring
occur together; both patients belong to the risk set just before that time. The survival
probabilities are `(5/6)`, `(5/6)*(4/5)` and `(5/6)*(4/5)*(1/2)` at times 1, 2 and 4.

```{r hand-km}
cohort <- data.frame(
  time = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5),
  event = c(1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0)
)
result <- jsurvival::singlearm(
  data = cohort, elapsedtime = "time", outcome = "event", outcomeLevel = "1",
  dod = NULL, dooc = NULL, awd = NULL, awod = NULL,
  timetypeoutput = "months", cutp = "1, 2, 4", person_time = TRUE
)
km <- result$survTable$asDF
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(km$surv, c(5/6, 2/3, 1/3))))
km
```

Total follow-up is 17 person-months and there are three events. The crude rate is
`100 * 3/17`, or about 17.65 per 100 person-months. This is not a percentage risk.
Exact Poisson limits concern the count/rate model and do not remove informative censoring
or population differences. A zero-event interval can have a positive upper confidence limit.

```{r hand-rate}
rate <- result$personTimeTable$asDF
expected_ci <- c(stats::qchisq(.025, 2 * 3),
                 stats::qchisq(.975, 2 * (3 + 1))) / (2 * 17) * 100
stopifnot(
  rate$events[1] == 3,
  rate$person_time[1] == 17,
  isTRUE(all.equal(rate$rate[1], 100 * 3/17)),
  isTRUE(all.equal(c(rate$rate_ci_lower[1], rate$rate_ci_upper[1]), expected_ci))
)
rate
```

Report the multiplier and time unit, the eligible cohort and censoring rules. Different
follow-up patterns and case mixes can change crude rate comparisons even when the rate
denominators are arithmetically correct. Median follow-up uses reverse Kaplan-Meier;
it is distinct from median survival and median observed time.

## Prepare endpoints and times together

Define which events count for OS, PFS, DFS, RFS or TTP in the study protocol; these names
alone do not specify every clinical rule. Outcome Organizer combines indicators but
cannot derive the earliest recurrence/death time. A composite indicator must be paired
with time to its first qualifying event. Do not pair recurrence-or-death status with
time to death when recurrence occurred earlier.

An unknown vital status stays unknown until verified. Administrative censoring truncates
follow-up at a fixed date and keeps qualifying events on or before that date. Check the
origin, date convention, timezone, last verified event-free assessment and follow-up end.
The interval calculator defaults to calendar months/years and also offers standardized
durations. Fixed divisions of days by 365.25 or 30.4375 use the latter convention.
Precalculated times are never converted just by
changing the output-unit selector.

Landmark analyses condition on observation beyond the landmark, exclude exact ties, and
subtract the landmark from retained times. They answer a conditional question and do not
implement delayed entry. Standard survival analyses disclose zero-time events; LASSO Cox
requires strictly positive follow-up. Do not add an arbitrary constant to make data fit.

## Preserve scaling and cutoff definitions

Continuous age per decade is `age / 10`, so its HR refers to a ten-year increase. Rounding
age down to a decade changes the predictor into bins. Ordinal factors in the standard
Cox analyses are represented as level comparisons; that is not an assumed linear trend.

For a cutoff selected by `survivalcont`, the grouping rule is **Low ≤ cutoff; High > cutoff**.
Use the unrounded value and the same equality rule for a held-out cohort:

```{r cutoff-equality}
cutoff <- 15.2
marker <- c(15.1, 15.2, 15.3, NA_real_)
group <- ifelse(marker > cutoff, "High", "Low")
stopifnot(identical(group, c("Low", "Low", "High", NA_character_)))
```

The single optimal-cutoff table includes a search-adjusted p-value. That adjustment does
not correct the optimism of the selected group HR. Outcome-guided multiple cutoffs have
unadjusted inferential comparisons. Keep a continuous model when it answers the research
question, and validate a selected threshold in patients who did not influence its selection.

## Separate model fitting, tuning and validation

A Cox HR is a relative instantaneous hazard. An interaction main effect applies at the
reference/zero value of the other term; it is not an overall average effect. Assess PH
and the functional form of continuous predictors. Sparse events, missingness, collinearity
and overfitting can undermine a numerically successful fit.

LASSO cross-validation selects lambda. The displayed C-index and risk groups use the
development patients and are apparent performance. The C-index ranges from 0 to 1 when
comparable pairs exist, with chance ordering at 0.5; it measures ordering, not calibration.
An empty LASSO model is a valid result. Conventional post-selection p-values and confidence
intervals are withheld. For performance validation repeat preprocessing, selection and
tuning within resampling, then assess the frozen model externally. Fixed event-count rules
do not establish sufficient sample size ([Riley et al., 2020](https://www.bmj.com/content/368/bmj.m441.short)).

Survival Analysis adjusted curves use the same fitted model and complete-case cohort
as the age-adjusted table. Baseline strata and age-group strata are retained under
every group assignment. Patient predictions are aligned on a common time grid before
averaging; curves end at the shortest observed stratum follow-up, so an unsupported
late plateau does not enter the average. Confidence bands for these standardized
averages are not provided. Recalculate saved adjusted curves from earlier candidates.

Multivariable Survival interaction forest plots show all fitted coefficients with their
95% confidence intervals, conditioning values and a caption. Both styles use this
coefficient display when interactions are present. A main effect applies at the stated
reference/zero values; an interaction row is a ratio of hazard ratios. Retain the caption
with the figure, including any warning that a conditioning value is outside the data.
Non-estimable coefficients are labelled without an estimate or interval.

## Reporting checklist

- Cohort, exclusions, missingness, number of patients and events, and unit of analysis.
- Endpoint definition, event/censor coding, time origin, unit/convention, and landmark if used.
- Estimand and estimator, uncertainty method, risk sets and follow-up support at reported times.
- Covariate units, factor references, interactions, PH assessment and adjustment variables.
- Whether cutoffs were prespecified or selected, search correction, exact threshold and tie rule.
- Model candidate set, penalty rule, seed/folds, apparent versus validated performance, and limitations.
- Module version and reproducible options; interpretation in the study's clinical context.
